lessons.title: Why Quantum Machine Learning Is an Open Research Question

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself precisely: a colleague says 'quantum machine learning will make our fraud-detection model faster and more accurate.' Write the two specific questions you'd ask before accepting that claim (e.g. compared to which classical baseline, and is this a peer-reviewed/reproduced result or a vendor claim). Then classify which of the lesson's four QML research threads (quantum algorithms for classical ML, variational circuits, quantum kernels, quantum-native ML) this course actually focuses on and why.
slots.deliverable: Your two written follow-up questions for the colleague's fraud-detection claim, plus a written identification of which two QML research threads this course covers and why those are the NISQ-runnable ones.

lessons.title: Classical ML Recap: What QML Is Trying to Augment

slots.practicalActivity: Reproduce the lesson's gradient descent example by hand for one more step: starting from theta=1.08 (the lesson's result after 2 steps) with L(theta)=(theta-3)^2 and eta=0.1, compute the gradient and the new theta. Then answer the Check Yourself: explain why the parameter moved by a smaller amount on the second step (0.48) than the first (0.6) even though eta stayed fixed.
slots.deliverable: Your hand-computed third gradient-descent step starting from theta=1.08, plus a written explanation of why the step size shrinks as theta approaches the minimum even with a constant learning rate.

lessons.title: The QML Toolchain: PennyLane & Qiskit Machine Learning

slots.practicalActivity: If you have Python available, pip install pennylane and define a simple one-qubit QNode (RY rotation, measure PauliZ) on the default.qubit device, then call qml.grad on it to confirm it returns a gradient. If you don't have a Python environment handy, instead build the lesson's shared-vocabulary table from memory (Device/Ansatz/Feature map/QNode mappings between PennyLane and Qiskit ML terms) and check it against the lesson.
slots.deliverable: Either your working PennyLane QNode with a confirmed qml.grad output, or your from-memory PennyLane/Qiskit-ML vocabulary table checked against the lesson's version.

lessons.title: Honest Framing: No Proven Practical Advantage Yet

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself: a vendor claims their quantum classifier 'beats classical ML by 20% on fraud detection.' List three specific questions from this lesson's five overclaiming patterns you'd ask before accepting that claim (e.g. was the classical baseline strong and comparably tuned, was this independently reproduced, does the comparison account for classical simulation cost).
slots.deliverable: Your written list of three specific, lesson-grounded questions you'd pose to the vendor before accepting the 20% improvement claim.

lessons.title: What a Variational Circuit Actually Is

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself by hand: for RY(theta)|0> measured in the Z basis, compute <Z> at theta=0 (RY(0)|0> = [cos(0),sin(0)] = [1,0], so <Z> = 1^2 - 0^2 = 1), and explain what that tells you about what RY(0) does to the state. Then reproduce the lesson's theta=pi/3 calculation independently (cos(pi/6) and sin(pi/6)) and confirm normalization sums to 1.0.
slots.deliverable: Your hand-computed <Z> at theta=0 with an explanation that RY(0) is the identity, plus your independently reproduced normalization check for theta=pi/3.

lessons.title: Parameterized Quantum Circuits as Trainable Models

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself with real arithmetic: for a 4-qubit ansatz with 3 layers, each layer applying both RY and RZ to every qubit, compute the total trainable parameter count (4 qubits x 2 rotations x 3 layers = 24), then compute how that number changes if a 4th layer were added (4 x 2 x 4 = 32).
slots.deliverable: Your two hand-computed parameter counts (24 for 3 layers, 32 for 4 layers) with the multiplication shown explicitly.

lessons.title: The Parameter-Shift Rule

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself by hand: for g(theta)=sin(theta), compute g(pi/2+pi/2)=sin(pi)=0 and g(pi/2-pi/2)=sin(0)=0, apply the parameter-shift formula [g(theta+pi/2)-g(theta-pi/2)]/2 to get the gradient at theta=pi/2, and check it against the calculus derivative g'(theta)=cos(theta) at theta=pi/2 (which is 0). Confirm both methods agree.
slots.deliverable: Your hand-computed parameter-shift gradient for sin(theta) at theta=pi/2, confirmed to match the calculus derivative cos(pi/2)=0.

lessons.title: Barren Plateaus: a Real Training Obstacle

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself in writing: a colleague proposes scaling a variational classifier from 6 qubits to 60 qubits using the same randomly-initialized, generic hardware-efficient ansatz, expecting proportionally better accuracy. Name the specific, documented obstacle (barren plateaus, citing McClean et al. 2018's exponential gradient-variance shrinkage) you'd raise, and list two things you'd ask them to show before believing training will succeed (e.g. gradient variance measurements at that qubit count, whether they're using local cost functions or problem-inspired ansatze).
slots.deliverable: A written warning citing the McClean et al. barren-plateau result by name, plus two specific concrete things you'd ask the colleague to demonstrate before trusting the 60-qubit scaling plan.

lessons.title: Variational Circuits Lab

slots.practicalActivity: Reproduce the lesson's full 3-iteration training trace by hand: starting at theta0=pi/3 with L(theta)=cos^2(theta) and eta=0.4, compute the loss and gradient at each of the 3 iterations, confirming your numbers match the lesson's table (loss 0.25 -> 0.0311 -> 0.0015). Then answer the Check Yourself: explain why the shrinking gradient magnitude here is a GOOD sign of genuine convergence, not a barren-plateau warning.
slots.deliverable: Your independently reproduced 3-iteration convergence table matching the lesson's loss and gradient values, plus a written explanation of why shrinking gradient near a true optimum differs from a barren plateau.

lessons.title: Encoding Classical Data Into Quantum States

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself by hand: amplitude-encode the classical vector (0, 3, 4, 0) into a 2-qubit state. Compute the norm (sqrt(0+9+16+0)=5), the normalized amplitude vector (0, 0.6, 0.8, 0), and identify which two computational basis states end up with nonzero amplitude.
slots.deliverable: Your hand-computed normalized amplitude vector for (0,3,4,0) confirming (0, 0.6, 0.8, 0), with the two nonzero basis states explicitly named.

lessons.title: Angle Encoding vs. Amplitude Encoding

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself: for a dataset with 8 continuous features, compute the qubit count needed under angle encoding (8) versus amplitude encoding (log2(8)=3). Then write the specific question you'd need to answer about the data's structure before concluding amplitude encoding is actually the better practical choice (i.e. does efficient state-preparation exist for this specific data, or would gate count erase the qubit savings).
slots.deliverable: Your computed qubit counts (8 vs 3) for the 8-feature dataset under each encoding, plus the specific follow-up question about state-preparation gate cost you'd need answered before choosing amplitude encoding.

lessons.title: Building a Variational Quantum Classifier

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself by hand: for a trained circuit outputting <Z>=-0.8 on a sample with true label y=0, compute the predicted probability p=(-0.8+1)/2=0.1, then compute the binary cross-entropy loss L=-[0*log(p)+(1-0)*log(1-p)]=-log(0.9), and determine whether this is a well-calibrated prediction.
slots.deliverable: Your hand-computed p=0.1 and binary cross-entropy loss (approximately 0.105) for the <Z>=-0.8, y=0 case, with a written judgment on whether the prediction is well-calibrated.

lessons.title: Quantum Kernel Methods

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself by hand: using k(x,x')=cos^2((x-x')/2), compute k(0, pi/2) and explain in words what a kernel value of exactly 0.5 means about the similarity of these two encoded points relative to k(x,x)=1 (identical) and k(x,x+pi)=0 (orthogonal).
slots.deliverable: Your hand-computed k(0, pi/2)=0.5 with a written explanation of what that intermediate similarity value means relative to the identical and orthogonal extremes.

lessons.title: Quantum Classifier Lab

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself by hand: using k(x,x')=cos^2((x-x')/2), compute k(D,A) and k(D,B) for a new test point D at x=1.0, given A at x=0.4 and B at x=0.5. Determine which training point D is more similar to and check whether that matches your intuition about where x=1.0 sits relative to 0.4 and 0.5.
slots.deliverable: Your hand-computed k(D,A) and k(D,B) values for D at x=1.0, with a written determination of which point D is more similar to and whether that matches geometric intuition.

lessons.title: Quantum Neural Network Architectures

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself in writing: a student says 'a QNN with 10 layers should be strictly more powerful than a VQC with 1 layer, the same way a 10-layer classical neural network beats a 1-layer one.' Using this lesson's point about the missing nonlinear activation function analogue, explain specifically what's incomplete about that comparison.
slots.deliverable: A written explanation of why the classical depth-equals-power intuition doesn't transfer cleanly to QNNs, citing the absence of a quantum activation-function analogue.

lessons.title: Training a Quantum Neural Network

slots.practicalActivity: Reproduce the lesson's 2-parameter worked example by hand: for f(theta1,theta2)=cos(theta1)+sin(theta2) at theta1=theta2=pi/4, compute the parameter-shift gradient for each parameter independently and confirm both match the lesson's -0.7071 and 0.7071 results. Then answer the Check Yourself: a QNN's loss curve is flat from iteration 1 using only 50 shots -- name two distinct explanations and one experiment to distinguish them.
slots.deliverable: Your independently reproduced two gradient computations (theta1 and theta2) matching the lesson's values, plus your written two-explanation list and distinguishing experiment for the flat-loss-curve scenario.

lessons.title: Quantum Convolutional Circuits: Overview

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself in writing: a paper claims 'QCNNs are the quantum version of CNNs, so they should be at least as good at image classification.' Using the distinction between quantum-data tasks (what Cong, Choi, and Lukin actually demonstrated -- classifying quantum phases of matter) and classical-data tasks (image classification), explain specifically what's wrong with that reasoning.
slots.deliverable: A written rebuttal distinguishing the proven quantum-phase-classification result from the unproven classical-image-classification claim, naming the original Cong/Choi/Lukin result specifically.

lessons.title: Quantum Neural Network Lab

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself by reasoning through the mechanism: explain why entanglement's effect shows up immediately on qubit 2 (the target) after just one CNOT layer, but qubit 1 (the control) only starts showing mixed measurement statistics once a second rotation+CNOT layer is added. Name the specific property of CNOT (it never changes the control's own marginal probabilities) that explains the asymmetry.
slots.deliverable: A written explanation of the control-vs-target asymmetry after one CNOT layer, citing the specific CNOT property (control-marginal invariance) that causes it.

lessons.title: Classical-Quantum Hybrid Training Loops

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself in writing: a colleague says 'we're building a fully quantum machine learning pipeline, with no classical computation anywhere in the loop.' Based on this lesson's 6-step hybrid loop trace, explain why that claim is not accurate for any currently practiced QML approach, naming the specific classical steps (loss computation, gradient assembly, optimizer state updates) that have no known quantum equivalent.
slots.deliverable: A written rebuttal of the 'fully quantum, zero classical computation' claim, naming the specific classical steps in the hybrid loop that currently have no quantum alternative.

lessons.title: Integrating QML With PyTorch or TensorFlow

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself in writing: explain why it matters practically that TorchLayer returns a parameter-shift-computed gradient to PyTorch's autograd 'as if' it came from ordinary backpropagation, and what would break (or become far more tedious) if PennyLane instead required you to manually intercept the backward pass every time. Then sketch the lesson's 3-stage hybrid sandwich architecture (classical -> quantum -> classical) for a hypothetical 6-feature dataset of your own choosing.
slots.deliverable: A written explanation of why autograd-compatible gradient return matters for usability, plus your own sketched 3-stage hybrid architecture for a 6-feature dataset you invented.

lessons.title: When a Hybrid Model Is — and Isn't — Worth the Complexity

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself by applying its 5-item decision checklist to the scenario it poses: a research project classifying small, carefully curated 4-feature datasets known to be hard for classical kernels, with an explicit classical-baseline comparison planned. Walk through all 5 checklist items for this scenario and determine whether it's a stronger or weaker case than the lesson's own fraud-detection example, naming which specific items make the difference.
slots.deliverable: Your full 5-item checklist walkthrough for the 4-feature research-project scenario, with a written determination of why it's a stronger case than fraud detection and which specific checklist items differ.

lessons.title: Hybrid Workflow Lab

slots.practicalActivity: Reproduce the lesson's full hybrid forward-and-backward pass by hand: with w=1.25, r=0.8, y=1, compute x=w*r, <Z>=cos(x), p=(<Z>+1)/2, loss, then the three chained gradients (dL/d<Z>, d<Z>/dx via parameter-shift, dx/dw), and the updated w. Verify (per the Check Yourself) that the new p is indeed higher than the original p, and explain in one sentence why higher p is correct given y=1.
slots.deliverable: Your fully reproduced hand calculation of the forward pass, three chained gradients, and updated weight, plus written verification that the new p exceeds the original and why that direction is correct for y=1.

lessons.title: Project Kickoff: Choosing a Real Dataset

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself in writing: explain why choosing a brand-new, never-before-studied dataset would actually make it HARDER, not easier, to satisfy the fair-comparison standard for this capstone project (no established classical baseline to compare against, no way to sanity-check your pipeline against published tutorial results). Then verify the qubit-budget check yourself: confirm that Iris reduced to 2 features needs exactly 2 qubits under angle encoding.
slots.deliverable: A written explanation of why a novel dataset would undermine fair comparison for this project, plus your own confirmation of the 2-qubit budget for the 2-feature Iris reduction.

lessons.title: Project: Build & Train a Quantum Classifier

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself with reasoning: the gradient step in this lesson only updated theta1 using the Setosa sample. Explain why updating theta1 using only the Versicolor sample's gradient instead could plausibly push theta1 in a different direction, and why a real training loop needs to account for every sample (not just one) before drawing any conclusion about the model's quality.
slots.deliverable: A written explanation of why single-sample gradients can conflict across different training examples, and why full-dataset training is required before judging a model's performance.

lessons.title: Project: Benchmark Against a Classical Baseline

slots.practicalActivity: Answer the lesson's Check Yourself precisely: the quantum classifier predicted class 0 for every single held-out sample. Trace this back to which sample's gradient was used in the previous lesson's single training step (Setosa only), explain specifically why that produces a classifier biased toward predicting 0 universally, and write what you would need to do differently (train on both classes across multiple iterations) to prevent this exact failure mode.
slots.deliverable: A written trace of the all-zeros-prediction failure back to the Setosa-only gradient step, plus a written description of the specific training change needed to fix it.

lessons.title: Project Wrap-Up: Honest Results Reporting

slots.practicalActivity: Complete the lesson's own Check Yourself as your capstone deliverable: write a 3-4 sentence honest summary of this project's result (quantum classifier 50% vs. classical baseline 100%, with the specific undertraining cause) that a skeptical reader who has completed this entire course would find both accurate and genuinely informative, explicitly distinguishing what you measured from what you can conclude -- following the lesson's 5-part honest-reporting template.
slots.deliverable: Your written 3-4 sentence honest project summary, structured to distinguish exact measured numbers from the limited scope of what they do and don't generalize to, following the lesson's reporting template.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course, a student can build and train real variational quantum circuits and quantum kernels using the parameter-shift rule, understands the proven barren-plateau obstacle and other real training limits, has built a hybrid classical-quantum classifier on a real dataset and honestly benchmarked it against a classical baseline, and can read a QML paper or vendor claim critically enough to spot common overclaiming patterns rather than repeating unverified advantage claims.
